system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Standard chase
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Chase steps for tgds and egds (triggers, active triggers, failure) and the nondeterministic fair algorithm. Also covers termination classes, undecidability, and homomorphic equivalence of the finite results. Excludes the other chase variants beyond the contrasts the book draws.

ATOMS:
- CS-DB-C01-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: The standard-chase algorithm iteratively applies standard-chase steps for active tgd or egd triggers. It stops with failure when an egd step fails, and it returns the current instance when no active trigger remains.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0016-s13] This algorithm can be described as an iterative application of the standard-chase steps.
    [CS-DB-p0016-s14] In case one of the egd chase steps fails, then the algorithm will fail.
    [CS-DB-p0016-s16] The algorithm terminates when either one of the egd chase step fails or when there are no other active triggers.
- CS-DB-C01-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: The standard-chase algorithm repeatedly applies standard-chase steps, nondeterministically choosing an active tgd or egd trigger each time. It stops when an egd step fails or when no active trigger remains.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0016-s13] This algorithm can be described as an iterative application of the standard-chase steps.
    [CS-DB-p0016-s15] If the algorithm does not fail, it nondeterministically chooses another active trigger, tgd or egd, and proceeds with the corresponding standard-chase step.
    [CS-DB-p0016-s16] The algorithm terminates when either one of the egd chase step fails or when there are no other active triggers.
- CS-DB-C01-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A standard-chase step with a tgd fires an active trigger $(\xi,h)$ by transforming $I$ into $J=I\cup\tilde h(\beta(\bar x,\bar z))$, where $\tilde h$ extends $h$ by assigning new fresh nulls to the existential variables of the head.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0014-s09] In case we also have that there is no extension ˜h of h such that ˜h(β(¯x, ¯z)) ⊆I, then (ξ, h) is said to be an active trigger for I.
    [CS-DB-p0014-s11] To ﬁre the trigger (ξ, h) means to transform I into the instance J = I ∪˜h(β(¯x, ¯z)), where ˜h is a distinct extension of h, i.e. an extension of h that assigns new fresh nulls to the existential variables in β.
    [CS-DB-p0014-s14] In case (ξ, h) is an active trigger for I, the transformation is called (ξ,h) standard-chase step and is denoted I −−−→J.
- CS-DB-C01-S1-04.r1a | S2
  ATOM: An egd $\alpha(\bar x)\to x_i=x_j$ is applicable to an instance $I$ with a homomorphism $h$ when $h$ maps the atoms of $\alpha(\bar x)$ to tuples of $I$ and $h(x_i)\neq h(x_j)$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0015-s19] We say that ξ is applicable to I with the homomorphism h, if the following holds: 1. h maps the atoms of α(¯x) to tuples of I, 2. h(xi)̸ = h(xj).
- CS-DB-C01-S1-04.r1b | S2
  ATOM: An egd chase step $(\xi,h)$ fails if $h$ maps both $x_i$ and $x_j$ to constants.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0015-s22] In case h maps both variables xi and xj to constants, then we say that the egd (ξ,h) chase step fails, and represent this by I −−−→⊥.
- CS-DB-C01-S1-04.r1c | S2
  ATOM: In a non-failing egd chase step, if $h(x_i)$ and $h(x_j)$ are both labeled nulls, the resulting instance $J$ is obtained from $I$ by replacing all occurrences of $h(x_i)$ with $h(x_j)$ (given an enumeration of the variables with $i<j$); if one is a constant and the other a labeled null, $J$ is obtained by replacing all occurrences of the null with the constant.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0015-s23] Otherwise, we say that the egd chase step (ξ,h) does not fail and denote this by I −−−→J, where instance J is computed as follows: 1. if both h(xi) and h(xj) are labeled nulls, then J is obtained from I by replacing all occurrences of h(xi) with h(xj), considering that there is an enumeration of the variables such that i < j. 2. if either h(xi) or h(xj) is a constant and the other is a labeled null, then J is obtained from I by replacing all occurrences of the labeled null with the constant.
- CS-DB-C01-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: If two finite instances $K$ and $J$ are returned by the standard-chase algorithm on two distinct execution branches with the same input $I$ and $\Sigma$, then $K$ and $J$ are homomorphically equivalent.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0018-s03] The following proposition shows the relationship between the ﬁnite instances returned by the algorithm. ▶Proposition 8. [19] If K and J are two ﬁnite instances returned by the standard-chase algorithm on two distinct execution branches, with input I and Σ, then K and J are homomorphically equivalent, that is K ↔J.
- CS-DB-C01-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Any finite instance returned by the standard-chase algorithm on an instance $I$ and a set $\Sigma$ of tgds and egds is a universal model of $I$ and $\Sigma$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0038-s03] Then any ﬁnite instance returned by the standard-chase algorithm is a universal model of I and Σ.
- CS-DB-C01-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: The standard-chase algorithm chooses nondeterministically which active trigger to apply at each step, so its execution can be viewed as a tree of branches and different branches may return different instances.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0016-s20] Note that the previous algorithm introduces a nondeterministic step at line 2, induced by the trigger choice.
    [CS-DB-p0016-s21] This makes the chase process to be viewed as a tree, where level i in the tree represents the i-th step in the chase algorithm, and where to each node a new edge is added for each of the applicable active trigger.
    [CS-DB-p0016-s22] Each path from the root of the tree to a leaf node represents an execution branch, or simply a branch, similarly to the nondeterministic ﬁnite automata.
    [CS-DB-p0016-s23] Thus the algorithm may return diﬀerent instances depending on the considered branch.
- CS-DB-C01-S3-01.r1 | S3
  ATOM: The standard chase is not complete for finding universal models: for an example instance $I$ and dependency set $\Sigma$ with $\xi_1 = R(x,y)\to\exists z\,R(y,z)$ and $\xi_2 = R(x,y),R(y,z)\to R(y,y)$, the standard chase has no terminating branch, although $\{R(a,b),R(b,b)\}$ is a universal model of $I$ and $\Sigma$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0038-s16] ξ1 = R(x, y) →∃z R(y, z), and ξ2 = R(x, y), R(y, z) →R(y, y).
    [CS-DB-p0038-s17] It is easy to see that there is no terminating branch for the standard chase for Σ and I.
    [CS-DB-p0038-s19] On the other hand, there exists universal model J = {R(a, b), R(b, b)} of I and Σ.
    [CS-DB-p0038-s20] Thus the standard chase is not complete in ﬁnding universal models.
- CS-DB-C01-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Testing whether a given set of tgds $\Sigma$ belongs to the class $CT^{std}_{\forall\exists}$, i.e., whether for every instance at least one standard-chase sequence is finite, is coRE-complete and hence undecidable.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0018-s21] More recently, Grahne and O. [26] extended this undecidability result to the CTstd∀∃class too.
    [CS-DB-p0018-s22] That is for a given Σ, the problem of testing if Σ ∈CTstd∀∃is coRE-complete.
- CS-DB-C01-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: For a given set $\Sigma$ of tgds, testing whether $\Sigma$ belongs to the class of tgd sets for which, on every instance, at least one standard-chase sequence is finite is coRE-complete, so standard-chase termination is undecidable in general.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DB-p0018-s21] More recently, Grahne and O. [26] extended this undecidability result to the CTstd∀∃class too.
    [CS-DB-p0018-s22] That is for a given Σ, the problem of testing if Σ ∈CTstd∀∃is coRE-complete.
